t4sd-range-construction: Short-Deck Ranges: Different Structure, Same Logic

The basic logic of range construction is unchanged in short deck (divide by hand strength into value/medium/bluffs), but the structure differs: pair density is higher (8.6% vs 5.9%), flush value rises, and the AK-vs-pair relationship shifts. Result: "pairs and suited hands" weigh more in short-deck ranges, while "pure big high cards (offsuit AK/AQ)" fall in relative value.

Short-deck range feature: pairs and suited hands are more valuable; offsuit big high cards relatively devalue. When constructing ranges, allocate more combos to pairs/suited connectors and reduce reliance on "offsuit AX".

Short-deck preflop range tiers (adjusted from standard hold'em):

Top: AA / KK / QQ (pairs are valuable and dominate AK)
Secondary value: JJ-TT / AK (strongest non-pair) / big pairs
Speculative tier: 66-99 (set mining, trips value) / suited connectors JTs+ / suited Ax

Versus standard hold'em:
In hold'em AK is upper-secondary value; in short deck AK is still secondary but below pairs
In hold'em suited connectors are the speculative tier; in short deck, with flush value up, they stay speculative but pay better

Polarization: short-deck betting ranges are more polarized (nut pairs + flush draws/bluffs) because draw density is high and made-hand value is large. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker range construction and 6+ structure)

Short-deck range practice differs: because draw density is high and made-hand value is large (flushes/straights), short-deck ranges can be more "polarized" — bet value with strong made hands (pairs/two pair/flushes), semi-bluff with strong draws (flush/straight draws), and check-control medium hands. Some "medium hands" in standard hold'em are better checked in short deck because their RIO is high.

Example: Short deck, BTN opens and you (BB) hold T♠9♠. T9s belongs to the speculative tier in short-deck ranges: it can make a flush (beats full houses) and straights. Chase draws actively postflop. Holding A♠K♦ (offsuit) instead, it's secondary value — can make top pair, but with high pair density on the flop, top pair is worth less than in standard hold'em.

Example 2 (polarized range): Short-deck flop 8♥7♥6♠, you (BTN IP) hold two pair (87) and a flush draw (A♥9♥). Two pair bets value (not the nuts in short deck but strong), the flush draw semi-bluffs. Medium hands (like 99) have high RIO on wet boards and are better checked. Short-deck range polarization makes the opponent hard to play against.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck ranges being more polarized doesn't mean "more aggressive into chaos". Polarization means strengthening "value/bluffs" and checking "medium hands" — because medium hands have high RIO on wet short-deck boards. When both extremes of the range are strong and the middle is empty, the opponent finds you hard to play against.

Short-deck range quick memory: top pairs + secondary AK + speculative pairs/suited connectors. Betting ranges are polarized (value pairs + semi-bluff draws); medium hands check-control. For every hand, first build your bet/check ratio by "which boards does my range dominate".
t4sd-equity: Short deck is a 6-max game, but with high draw density, multiway pots dilute equity (Equity) significantly. In multiway pots your top pair/two pair face multiple opponents' draws and the win rate gets carved up; the risk of a flush/straight draw's "one of my outs gives another opponent a stronger hand" rises. Understanding equity dilution is the foundation of short-deck multiway decisions.

Short-deck multiway equity rule: every extra opponent dilutes your made-hand equity. Top pair/two pair drop in value multiway, and draws lose "cleanliness" (may feed a stronger hand) — tighten and pot-control in multiway pots.

Multiway equity dilution example (short deck):

Heads-up: you hold top pair vs a single range, about 60%-70%
Three-way: add one more opponent, your top pair may drop to 35%-45%

Draw out "cleanliness":
Multiway, your flush-draw outs may be held by another opponent / make a bigger flush, losing value

Equity sums: heads-up U₁+U₂=100%, three-way U₁+U₂+U₃=100%
Your share falls as opponents increase

Conclusion: multiway, the thin value of made hands (top pair/two pair) is diluted and draws' reverse implied odds rise. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker multiway equity and 6+ math)

Short-deck multiway practice: because pots are usually big and entry rates high, multiway pots are common. In multiway pots: (1) tighten marginal calls (top pair weak kicker's value is diluted); (2) fast-play strong hands (avoid giving multiple opponents free draws); (3) chase draws more cautiously (outs cleanliness drops, RIO rises).

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ on an A♦J♣8♥ flop (top pair top kicker) three-way. You have top pair of Aces but two opponents. Heads-up your top pair is strong (about 65%); three-way it may drop to 40%. One opponent holds a J, another an 8 or a draw — either can overtake you. The right play is to bet for protection (fast-play), but realize the bigger the pot, the more your thin value is diluted — control or reassess on the turn and river.

Example 2 (draw RIO): Short deck, you hold 7♥8♥ on a 9♦T♣A♠ flop, drawing to an open-ended straight (6/J), three-way. Your straight-draw outs get "diluted" multiway: if another opponent also draws 6/J, you split the pot or he makes a bigger straight. And if the turn brings the opponent two pair/trips, your straight can lose to bigger hands too. Chase draws more cautiously multiway.

Counterintuitive point: in short-deck multiway pots, "I have a strong draw so I chase" can become donating money. Because outs cleanliness drops (may feed a stronger hand) and RIO rises, your draw equity gets divided among many. Multiway pots are for "fast-playing strong hands + tightening draw chases", not "aggressive draw chasing".

Short-deck multiway quick memory: each extra opponent dilutes equity about 10%-20%. A heads-up 60% top pair is about 40% three-way. Multiway: fast-play strong hands for protection, tighten marginal calls, and judge draw chases by outs cleanliness.
t4sd-blockers: Short-Deck Blockers: A New Dimension of Hand Reading

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces specific opponent combos. Blockers have special value in short deck: because flush value is enormous (beats full houses) and pair density is high, blocking the opponent's flush/pair combos affects bluffing and calling decisions more. When you hold A♥, the opponent's A♥X♥ nut flush is completely blocked — extremely valuable in short deck.

Short-deck blocker rule: holding an A blocks the nut flush (opponent's A♥X♥ combos = 0); holding a pair blocks the opponent's pairs. Short-deck flushes/pairs are valuable, so blocking them massively impacts bluff success.
The Triple Application of Short-Deck Blockers

Short-deck blockers have triple value: (1) blocking flushes — holding A♠ zeros out the opponent's A♠X♠ nut flush, raising bluff success; (2) blocking pairs — holding a K drops the opponent's KK from 6 to 3 combos; (3) unblocking value — not holding a suit means the opponent is more likely to have a flush and pay your value bet. In short deck these blocking effects are amplified by the high value of flushes/pairs.

Example: Short-deck flop K♠9♠6♠ (three spades), you hold A♦A♣ (no spade A). You block no flushes — the opponent can have A♠X♠ nut flush or a smaller flush. Your AA's bluff-catching value drops; lean fold. Conversely, if you hold A♠ (no flush made), you block all A♠X♠ nut-flush combos and the opponent's "strongest hand" is falsified — your bluff or call success rises.

Example 2 (preflop blocking): Short deck, you (BB) face an SB open and consider a 3-bet bluff. The difference between A♦6♦ and 7♦6♦: A6s's A blocks the opponent's AA and AK (fewer top hands, lower 4Bet frequency), and after a 4Bet A6s folds cleanly; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often when 4Bet. Short-deck pair density is high, so the A blocker is more valuable.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck blockers are a marginal tool, not a master key. Holding A♠ raises bluff success but doesn't guarantee it; using it to overturn base range analysis is abuse. Blockers carry more weight in short deck (high flush/pair value) but remain the "icing after the base range is right".

Short-deck blocker quick memory: on a three-suited board holding A♠ → blocks the nut flush, bonus for bluffing/calling; holding a pair → blocks the opponent's pairs. Off-the-table drill: set up random three-suited boards and count "opponent nut-flush combos" with and without your A♠, until you can judge in 10 seconds in play.

t4sd-range-construction-q1.question: The main structural difference between short-deck and standard hold'em range construction is:
options: Higher pair density, higher flush value, offsuit big high cards relatively devalue
t4sd-range-construction-q1.explanation: Short deck has higher pair density (8.6%), higher flush value, and offsuit big high cards relatively devalue — different range structure.

t4sd-range-construction-q2.question: The speculative tier of a short-deck preflop range mainly includes:
options: 66-99 pairs + suited connectors JTs+ + suited Ax
t4sd-range-construction-q2.explanation: The short-deck speculative tier is small pairs (set mining) + suited connectors + suited Ax, exploiting trips and flush value.

t4sd-range-construction-q3.question: Why are short-deck betting ranges more "polarized"?
options: High draw density and large made-hand value, with medium hands better checked due to high RIO
t4sd-range-construction-q3.explanation: Short-deck draw density is high and made-hand value large; betting ranges use value pairs + semi-bluff draws, while medium hands check due to high RIO.

t4sd-range-construction-q4.question: Holding a medium hand (99) on a short-deck 8♥7♥6♠ flop, the correct play is:
options: Check for pot control — high RIO on a wet board
t4sd-range-construction-q4.explanation: Short-deck medium hands (99) have high RIO on wet boards — better to check and control than bet for value.

t4sd-range-construction-q5.question: The relative value of offsuit AK in short deck versus standard hold'em is:
options: Lower (high pair density makes top-pair value worse than standard hold'em)
t4sd-range-construction-q5.explanation: Short-deck pair density is high, so offsuit AK's top-pair value drops — relatively devalued.

t4sd-equity-q1.question: The main manifestation of equity dilution in short-deck multiway pots is:
options: Top pair/two pair win rates get carved up, and draw outs lose cleanliness
t4sd-equity-q1.explanation: Multiway, top pair/two pair win rates are divided among many, and draw outs may feed a stronger hand (losing cleanliness).

t4sd-equity-q2.question: A heads-up top pair is about 65%; three-way it may drop to:
t4sd-equity-q2.explanation: Each extra opponent dilutes equity; three-way top pair may drop to 35%-45%.

t4sd-equity-q3.question: In short-deck multiway pots, the correct handling of strong hands is:
options: Fast-play and bet for protection, avoiding giving multiple opponents free draws
t4sd-equity-q3.explanation: Multiway, multiple opponents may chase draws — strong hands should fast-play and bet for protection, avoiding free chases.

t4sd-equity-q4.question: Why should draw chases be more cautious in short-deck multiway pots?
options: Outs cleanliness drops (may feed a stronger hand) and RIO rises
t4sd-equity-q4.explanation: Multiway, draw outs may give another opponent a stronger hand and reverse implied odds rise — chase more cautiously.

t4sd-equity-q5.question: The correct play for marginal top pair weak kicker in short-deck multiway pots is:
options: Tighten or pot-control — thin value is diluted
t4sd-equity-q5.explanation: Multiway, top pair weak kicker's thin value is diluted — tighten or pot-control.

t4sd-blockers-q1.question: The special value of blockers in short deck comes from:
options: Extremely high flush value (beats full houses) and high pair density
t4sd-blockers-q1.explanation: Short-deck flushes are extremely valuable (beat full houses) and pair density is high — blocking flushes/pairs is amplified.

t4sd-blockers-q2.question: Holding A♠ on a three-spade board affects the opponent's nut-flush combos by:
options: Completely blocking them (A♠X♠ = 0), raising bluff success
t4sd-blockers-q2.explanation: Holding A♠ zeroes the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest call/raise-back hands and raising bluff success.

t4sd-blockers-q3.question: For a preflop 3-bet bluff, why is A5s better than 76s?
options: A5s blocks AA/AK, lowering the 4Bet frequency
t4sd-blockers-q3.explanation: A5s's A blocks the opponent's AA/AK, lowering 4Bet frequency; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often.

t4sd-blockers-q4.question: The applicability boundary of short-deck blockers is:
options: A marginal tool on edge spots, requiring a correct base range first
t4sd-blockers-q4.explanation: Blockers adjust combo ratios, not rewrite ranges — icing when the base range is right, unable to save you when the base is wrong.

t4sd-blockers-q5.question: Holding A♦A♣ (no spade A) on a three-spade board facing a bet, the correct tendency is:
options: Be cautious — you block no flushes, so his calling range skews strong
t4sd-blockers-q5.explanation: Without A♠ you block no flushes; he can have A♠X♠ nuts or a smaller flush, lowering your bluff-catching value.
